## Chapter 5 {#slide-1}

Common Parametric discrete random variables

Discrete Uniform Distribution

Bernoulli Distribution

Binomial distribution

Poisson distribution

## Motivation {#slide-2}

Many real-life experiments follow similar patterns:

Experiments with only two possible outcomes ('success', 'failure')

Experiments that involve a sequence of binary outcomes

Experiments that involve sampling without replacement

Experiments that involve counting occurrences over a given space or time

These random variables arising from these common experiments merit more formal  pmfs  and properties

These distributions are governed by parameters ,  which govern the  pmf , mean, variance, etc.

## Bernoulli distribution {#slide-10}

## Motivation {#slide-11}

Consider the following experiments:

Flip a coin.  Observe whether it lands heads or tails.

Shoot a basketball.  Observe whether you make or miss.

Hire a new CEO.  Observe whether the individual is male or female.

Roll a roulette wheel.  Observe whether it lands red or not.

## Poisson distribution {#slide-32}

## Motivation {#slide-33}

Consider experiments that measure counts per unit space or time

Examples

Number of cars at a drive-thru window in one hour

Number of accidents along a 0.5-mile stretch of highway

Number of tadpoles per cubic cm of pondwater

These random variables are often modeled with the  Poisson distribution

## Example 9 {#slide-41}

Customers arrive at a travel agency at a mean rate of 11 per hour. The agency would like to determine how many agents they need on hand. One agent is needed for every 3 people that walk through the door. 

Find the mean and variance.

Find the probability that at most 3 customers will arrive in a given hour.
